title: Revert a merge — and understand why re-merging then does nothing
summary: A merged feature broke production. Revert the merge with -m, then discover the trap: merging that branch again brings back nothing, because git thinks it is already in.
mental_model: Reverting a merge undoes its *content* but not its *topology* — the branch stays reachable, so git still considers it merged. Fixing the branch and merging again therefore brings in only the new commits, not the ones the revert undid.
danger: This is the most common way a feature silently half-disappears: reverted merge, branch fixed, re-merged, and the original work never comes back.

steps.title: Find the merge that shipped the problem
steps.why: A merge commit has two parents. `--parents` prints them, and that is what makes reverting it different from reverting anything else — git has to be told which side is 'the mainline'.

steps.title: Watch a plain revert refuse
steps.why: Without `-m`, git cannot know whether 'undo this merge' means 'remove the feature' or 'remove main's work'. It refuses rather than guessing — one of the few places git asks instead of assuming.
steps.expect: error: commit ... is a merge but no -m option was given.

steps.title: Revert against the first parent
steps.why: `-m 1` means 'keep the first parent's line, undo what the other side brought'. On a merge into main, parent 1 is always main — so `-m 1` is nearly always what you want.
steps.expect: payments.py is gone, and a Revert commit sits on top.

verify.label: the merged feature's content is undone

steps.title: Fix the branch
steps.why: The feature was not wrong in principle, only broken. Add the missing validation on the branch, as you would after any production revert.

steps.title: Merge it again and watch it go wrong
steps.why: Here is the trap. Git considers the old commits already merged — the revert changed content, not reachability — so it tries to apply only the new validation commit onto a tree where the file no longer exists. The result is a modify/delete conflict, not the feature coming back.
commands: git merge --no-ff -m "Merge fixed payments feature" feature/payments
steps.expect: A conflict, and not one that resolving would fix: the original charge and refund code is simply not in this merge.

verify.label: re-merging produced a conflict instead of restoring the feature

steps.title: Abort — this is the wrong route entirely
steps.why: No resolution of this conflict brings the original code back, because git is not offering it. Abort and fix the actual problem, which is the revert commit sitting in main's history.
steps.expect: Back to the reverted state: clean tree, no payments.py.

verify.label: the failed merge is fully undone

steps.title: Undo the revert instead
steps.why: The correct fix is to revert the revert: that reinstates the original content, so main once again matches what git believes about reachability. Now merging works from a truthful base.

verify.label: the original feature content is restored

steps.title: Now merge the fixed branch, successfully
steps.why: With the content restored, the merge does what you expected the first time: it brings in the validation commit and nothing conflicts. The order of operations was the whole problem.
commands: git merge --no-ff -m "Merge fixed payments feature" feature/payments
steps.expect: charge(), refund() and the validation, all present.

verify.label: the fix merged in cleanly once the revert was undone

steps.title: Read the history you produced
steps.why: Merged, reverted, fixed, restored, merged again — every step recorded, nothing rewritten, and anyone reading it can reconstruct exactly what happened during the incident.

verify.label: the feature is fully back, original code and fix together
verify.hint: revert -m 1 to undo the merge, then revert THAT commit to restore it

verify.label: the revert and its undo are both recorded in history
nothing was rewritten — this was all additive

pitfalls: `-m 1` is the mainline parent — the branch you merged INTO. `-m 2` undoes main's side instead, which is almost never what you want.
After reverting a merge, the branch still counts as merged. Always revert the revert before merging it again, or fix forward on a fresh branch.
An alternative is to fix forward: new branch, new commits, normal merge. On a busy repository this is often less confusing than the revert-the-revert dance.
Squash-merged branches do not have this problem, because there is no merge commit — and no reachability to confuse.
